chunks: "Maximum power gets delivered to the load when the load resistance equals the source resistance, R L equals R s .
If the source has a reactive part, the load impedance has to be the complex conjugate, Z L equals Z s^ , so the reactances cancel.
To see why, model the source as a voltage V s with series R s . The current is V s over (R s plus R L) and the load power is V s squared R L over (R s plus R L) squared .
If R L is tiny you get lots of current but almost no voltage across the load. If R L is huge you get voltage but no current.
The product peaks in the middle, and if you take the derivative and set it to zero you get R L equals R s . The maximum power is V s squared over (4R s) .
The catch is that at that point the source resistor dissipates just as much as the load, so efficiency is only 50%.
That's fine for something like an antenna or a sensor where the available power is tiny and you want to capture as much as you can, and it's why RF is matched to 50 ohms.
But for a power supply I want the opposite: a very low output resistance, so almost all of the power goes to the load and the voltage doesn't sag."
